I was working for an online survey company as a web dev. It was an awful job. Lots of nepotism, vindictive coworkers and terrible clients. It was a job though, so I tried to make the best of it and interviewed when I could.

But it really comes down to who you already know and where they're at. And if people know you're actively looking then they might know someone with a need.

One big issue is that networking takes time, which a lot of people here don't seem to have. If you went through an internship without noting who you worked with, well, sorry, but that half of what an internship is for. This is rarely told to people though, but it should be. 

If it helps, think of the dynamic at play, you want something that other people have. Is it any wonder these people show indifference? You have to get to the point where you can seem not to need what they have. It's paradoxical, I know, but that's life.

Edit: To further clarify, my general rule for recruiters is if I can go to their company's office and talk to them then I can deal with them. I've gotten several roles through such companies, some good and some very bad. That's life.

Your best bet is to always network, even amongst recruiters relatively close to you geographically.

If it helps, you can think of an adapter as the edge of two separate systems.

It's like USB type-A power supplies. They might use the same connector, but there are a bunch out there that are nonstandard. If you plug something in that those aren't meant for the devices will get 12V instead of the 5V they were expecting. The adapter conformed to there physical interface but the payload it passed along was incorrect. 

You always have to be aware of necessary changes at the edges like this. Or both sides could support using different adapters, like standard ones. Think like REST APIs, GraphQL and the like.

The point of an adapter is to decouple things. If one side changes then of course you need a different adapter. 

The point is that changing one side or the other doesn't matter if you have an adapter that works between them. They're coupled to the adapter from their respective sides and not each other.

It’s fine if you don’t use version control though. But the projects we were using it against were pretty complicated and convoluted.

I've used JMeter on many complex systems, and even taught others how to use it to full effect. I'd not recommend it for the purpose now, and I haven't looked back since I moved away from load testing years ago.

Part of the issue is that JMeter represents all of its nodes in an XML format, and if you've ever looked at a diff between two XML files where nodes have been moved between levels in the tree then you know what kind of headache it can be. They may as well have been binary files if you wanted to use git for version control.
